vignette: The phone rings on a Tuesday morning in Dubai. At sixty-three, Amira is reviewing a subsidiary's financial controls when her mother's voice fractures through the line. Her younger brother, Tariq, has collapsed at the gym. By the time Amira boards the night flight, his breathing has stopped. In the hospital corridor, she watches the nurses work with detached precision, cataloging the timing of the defibrillator pads, the sterile equipment, the exact minute they declare time of death. It is the only way she can keep from shattering. When they ask her to identify him, she signs the form with a steady hand. That hand, she will learn, becomes both her anchor and her cage. In the months that follow, Amira returns to her audit firm in London, but the work no longer flows. Spreadsheets blur into gray grids. She finds herself rereading the same cell for forty minutes, searching for a numerical discrepancy that never existed, as if a misplaced decimal could somehow reverse a timeline. Her auditing training demands absolute certainty, yet now every ledger feels like a puzzle missing its center. She begins auditing her own household-checking the stove three times, locking the door twice, measuring out her coffee with clinical exactness. The numbers used to reassure her. Now they only amplify the static. Her colleagues notice her withdrawal. She declines evening gatherings. When neighbors leave condolence cards, she answers her door just long enough to murmur thanks, then retreats behind the deadbolt. She lives alone in a quiet apartment, but the silence is never truly empty. Every Friday evening, she clears a place at her dining table, sets out a small plate of baklava from the Middle Eastern grocer downtown, and says his name into the kitchen. No one answers. She does not ask them to. The grief does not move in straight lines. It accumulates like unresolved entries in a ledger. Amira catches herself holding her breath while reviewing vendor contracts, her pulse jumping at the sudden screech of a subway brake, the sharp intake of air from a stranger's cough, the flash of a coffee cup tipping over. Her mind catalogs threats the way it once cataloged financial irregularities. Sleep offers no refuge. She lies awake, tracing ceiling patterns, replaying the hospital corridor in relentless loops, rehearsing conversations she wishes she had never left unsaid. When she finally drifts off, her body tenses, and she wakes before her alarm, certain she has overslept, certain she has missed something critical. Her work suffers. She double-checks email signatures. She avoids the grocery aisle where she once bought Tariq's favorite tea. She stops answering calls from family abroad. When a colleague pats her shoulder in the breakroom, she flinches, her vision tunneling until his voice breaks through the haze. The past does not feel distant; it occupies the same room as the present, breathing the same air. Yet, when she speaks of his laugh, the way he would mimic their mother's phrases in her old Damascene accent, her shoulders soften. Today, Amira sits in my office and explains that she no longer trusts her own memory. She shows up to work every day. She still audits. She still sets the table. And when the quiet in her apartment grows too heavy, she puts on her headphones, lets the city sounds rush in, and waits for the next hour to pass.
